Class SmartDateParser_v2

  • java.lang.Object
    • util.SmartDateParser_v2

  • public final class SmartDateParser_v2
extends java.lang.Object
    A flexible utility for converting date strings of varying formats into Date, LocalDateTime, and ZonedDateTime objects.

    Regional Support and Ambiguity: This parser is optimised for Australian/British/Indian (DD/MM/YYYY) date formats. In cases of numerical ambiguity, for example: 01/02/2026, the parser prioritises the Day-Month-Year interpretation (1st February). This default does not depend on the JVM's default locale.

    Month-first input (for example US): Callers who know their data is month-first can pass an input Locale to the overloads that accept one. If, according to the JDK's locale data, that locale's short date pattern starts with the month (for example Locale.US), numeric dates are read as Month-Day-Year, so 04/05/2026 becomes 5 April. Matching is strict: 23/04/2026 is then rejected rather than silently re-read as day-first. A null locale, or any locale whose short pattern does not start with the month, keeps the default Day-Month-Year order. Only purely numeric dates are affected; textual months, year-first dates and ISO-8601 strings are unambiguous and parse identically either way. The locale passed to the convertToLocalisedDateTime methods controls output formatting only and has no effect on how the input is read.

    Strictness: Parsing is strict. Impossible dates such as 31/02/2026 are rejected rather than being adjusted to the nearest valid date.

    Time zones: Input that carries an offset or region (ISO-8601) keeps it. Input without one is interpreted in the zone supplied by the caller, or the JVM default zone for the overloads that do not take a ZoneId. Callers parsing data that originates elsewhere (for example Asia/Kolkata) should always supply the source zone explicitly.

    Thread safety: This class is thread-safe. All shared state (Patterns and DateTimeFormatters) is immutable and created once in the static initialiser, and nothing is cached, so memory use is constant.

    Supported Date Formats
    Standard Format Pattern / Example Description
    ISO-8601 2026-04-23T20:00[:ss[.SSS]][Z|+05:30|+0530][[Region/Id]] T-delimited timestamps with optional seconds, fraction, offset and region.
    EXIF / Year first yyyy:MM:dd HH:mm:ss, yyyy-MM-dd Year-month-day with any of / - : . space as separator.
    Day first dd/MM/yyyy, d MMM yyyy, 23 April 2026 Numeric or textual month (abbreviated or full, case-insensitive).
    Year first, textual month yyyy MMM dd Common in professional software output.
    International/US MMM dd, yyyy or MMM dd yyyy Textual month first (e.g., Jan 19, 2026).

    Every non-ISO date may be followed by an optional time in 24-hour form (H:mm, H:mm:ss, H:mm:ss.SSS) or 12-hour form (h:mm a, h:mm:ss a, for example 08:30 PM).

    Not supported: two-digit years, timezone abbreviations such as IST, and offsets on non-ISO input. Input longer than 100 characters is rejected.

      • convertToDate

        public static java.util.Date convertToDate(java.lang.String input)
        Obtains a Date after parsing the specified input, interpreting offset-less input in the JVM default time zone.

        Provided for legacy APIs that require Date. Prefer convertToZonedDateTime(String, ZoneId) for new code.

        Parameters:
        input - the date string to convert
        Returns:
        the parsed timestamp, or null if the input is null, blank or an EXIF "zero date" (for example 0000:00:00 00:00:00)
        Throws:
        java.lang.IllegalArgumentException - if the input is too long, does not match any supported date format, or is not a valid date

        defaultZone - the zone applied when the input carries no offset or region

        java.lang.NullPointerException - if defaultZone is null

      • convertToLocalDateTime

        public static java.time.LocalDateTime convertToLocalDateTime(java.lang.String input)
        Parses a raw date string into a LocalDateTime exactly as written. No time zone is applied, so the result is never shifted by daylight saving gaps or overlaps. If the input carries an offset or region, it is ignored and the written wall-clock time is returned.
        Parameters:
        input - the raw date string to parse
        Returns:
        the parsed local date and time (start of day if no time was given), or null if the input is null, blank or an EXIF "zero date"
        Throws:
        java.lang.IllegalArgumentException - if the input is too long, does not match any supported date format, or is not a valid date

      • convertToZonedDateTime

        public static java.time.ZonedDateTime convertToZonedDateTime(java.lang.String input,
                                                             java.time.ZoneId defaultZone)
        Parses a raw date string into a ZonedDateTime.

        ISO-8601 input that carries an offset or region keeps it. All other input is interpreted in defaultZone. Supplying the source zone (for example Asia/Kolkata) avoids silently depending on the server's zone.

        Parameters:
        input - the raw date string
        defaultZone - the zone applied when the input carries no offset or region
        Returns:
        the parsed value, or null if the input is null, blank or an EXIF "zero date"
        Throws:
        java.lang.IllegalArgumentException - if the input is too long, does not match any supported date format, or is not a valid date; when a pattern recognised the input but parsing failed, the underlying DateTimeException is attached as the cause
        java.lang.NullPointerException - if defaultZone is null

      • convertToZonedDateTime

        public static java.time.ZonedDateTime convertToZonedDateTime(java.lang.String input,
                                                             java.time.ZoneId defaultZone,
                                                             java.util.Locale inputLocale)
        Parses a raw date string into a ZonedDateTime, using inputLocale to decide how ambiguous numeric dates such as 04/05/2026 are read.

        ISO-8601 input that carries an offset or region keeps it. All other input is interpreted in defaultZone.

        Parameters:
        input - the raw date string
        defaultZone - the zone applied when the input carries no offset or region
        inputLocale - a locale whose short date pattern starts with the month (for example Locale.US) reads numeric dates as Month-Day-Year; null or any other locale keeps the default Day-Month-Year order
        Returns:
        the parsed value, or null if the input is null, blank or an EXIF "zero date"
        Throws:
        java.lang.IllegalArgumentException - if the input is too long, does not match any supported date format, or is not a valid date; when a pattern recognised the input but parsing failed, the underlying DateTimeException is attached as the cause
        java.lang.NullPointerException - if defaultZone is null

      • convertToLocalisedDateTime

        public static java.lang.String convertToLocalisedDateTime(java.lang.String input,
                                                          java.util.Locale locale)
        Formats a raw date string as a localised, human-readable timestamp using the specified Locale.

        The locale controls the output only. The input is always read with the default Day-Month-Year order; to read month-first input, parse it with convertToZonedDateTime(String, ZoneId, Locale) and pass the result to convertToLocalisedDateTime(ZonedDateTime, Locale).

        Parameters:
        input - the raw date string to parse and format
        locale - the locale used for localisation rules, or null for the JVM default format locale
        Returns:
        the localised string, or null if the input is null, blank or an EXIF "zero date"
        Throws:
        java.lang.IllegalArgumentException - if the input is too long, does not match any supported date format, or is not a valid date

      • convertToLocalisedDateTime

        public static java.lang.String convertToLocalisedDateTime(java.time.ZonedDateTime dateTime,
                                                          java.util.Locale locale)
        Formats a ZonedDateTime as a localised, human-readable timestamp using MEDIUM date and SHORT time styles, for example 23 Apr 2026, 8:00 pm (en_AU).

        The formatter is created per call on purpose: a cache keyed by caller-supplied locales would be an unbounded map.

        The exact output is defined by the JDK's locale data and varies between versions, so avoid asserting on the literal string in tests.

        Parameters:
        dateTime - the date and time to format
        locale - the locale used for localisation rules, or null for the JVM default format locale
        Returns:
        the localised string, or null if dateTime is null; callers decide what to display for a missing value

                                                         java.util.Locale inputLocale)
        Core parser shared by all public entry points.
        Parameters:
        input - the raw, untrimmed caller input; may be null
        inputLocale - decides how ambiguous numeric dates are read; may be null (day-first)
        Returns:
        a ZonedDateTime if the input carried an offset or region, otherwise a LocalDateTime; or null for null, blank or EXIF zero-date input
        Throws:
        java.lang.IllegalArgumentException - if the input is too long or cannot be parsed

      • isMonthFirst

        private static boolean isMonthFirst(java.util.Locale locale)
        Decides whether numeric dates should be read month-first, from the first date field of the locale's short date pattern (for example M/d/yy for US English). The pattern comes from the JDK's locale data, so it can differ between JDK versions.
        Parameters:
        locale - the caller's input locale; may be null
        Returns:
        true only if the locale's short date pattern starts with the month; false for null and for every other pattern, which keeps the day-first default

      • buildFormatter

        private static java.time.format.DateTimeFormatter buildFormatter(java.lang.String order,
                                                                 boolean textualMonth,
                                                                 java.lang.String separator,
                                                                 boolean twelveHour)
        Builds a strict, case-insensitive formatter for one layout and separator. The 24-hour variant treats the time as optional (so it also handles date-only input); the 12-hour variant requires an AM/PM marker.
        Parameters:
        order - field order, using y, M and d
        textualMonth - true if the month is a name, false if it is a number
        separator - the literal placed between the date fields
        twelveHour - true for the mandatory 12-hour time variant, false for the optional 24-hour time variant
        Returns:
        an immutable, thread-safe formatter

      • appendMonth

        private static void appendMonth(java.time.format.DateTimeFormatterBuilder builder,
                                boolean textual)
        Appends a month field. Textual months accept the full name or the three-letter abbreviation; the full name is attempted first so that, for example, "March" is not consumed as "Mar".

        builder - the builder to append to
        textual - true for a month name, false for a one or two digit number
